safetyNote: Hydnum rufescens is included on the edible lists of DGfM and Swiss VAPKO. Eat only after confident identification and adequate cooking. Turn the cap over: the fertile surface has soft, fragile teeth, not gills; it is typically smaller and more orange-russet than the paler hedgehog H. repandum. The teeth usually stop before the stem, but that single character is not absolute. Genetic studies show that the traditional H. rufescens appearance covers several close species, so a drawing cannot confirm a strict species identification.

sections.title: Small terracotta cap
sections.text: The cap is commonly about 3–8 cm wide, orange, terracotta or light rusty red, often with a paler wavy edge. It is convex when young and may flatten or become shallowly depressed and irregular with age. Its surface is smooth to faintly felted, not covered in coarse wool. The stem is usually distinct from the cap, comparatively slender, pale cream to peach, and often roughly central, although its position varies. Flesh is pale and brittle.

sections.title: Teeth rather than gills
sections.text: The underside is covered with soft, fragile, downward-pointing pale cream to peach-orange teeth. They are generally attached near the stem but do not markedly run down it, unlike the often decurrent teeth of H. repandum; the degree of attachment varies and must not be used alone. Teeth readily break or rub off. A complete underside view is indispensable because the cap alone can resemble many ordinary gilled fungi.

sections.title: Woodland and close species
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal fungus occurs in both broadleaf and conifer woodland; European records include beech and spruce forests. It fruits in summer and autumn. The larger, paler H. repandum commonly has a more robust stem and teeth descending it. Other small russet Hydnum species can be nearly identical macroscopically; one study found six genetic lineages under the traditional H. rufescens name, and a later taxonomic revision recognised a wider diversity of Hydnum species. Exact names may require microscopy or sequencing.

sections.title: Edibility and limits of identification
sections.text: Both the German Society for Mycology and VAPKO list H. rufescens as a food mushroom. The overall Hydnum group is recognised by soft teeth, but species-level identification within the russet group can be difficult. Do not substitute a colour-only guess for the underside and whole-specimen examination. The illustration depicts the traditional field concept of H. rufescens and cannot resolve its hidden species diversity.

traits: Orange to terracotta-russet cap, commonly 3–8 cm, smooth to faintly felted with a sometimes wavy paler edge
Underside with short soft fragile pale cream-to-peach teeth, not gills
Teeth usually not conspicuously decurrent, but attachment varies
Slender distinct pale cream-to-peach stem, usually roughly central; pale brittle flesh
Broadleaf and conifer woodland, including beech and spruce sites, in summer and autumn
Part of a taxonomically complex group of similar russet Hydnum species
